 Strengthening India’s Healthcare System 
 Tags: GS Paper - 2 
 Health 
 Government Policies & Interventions 
 This editorial is based on " India's lower health spending burden still masks gaps in public care " published in the Business Standard on 17/11/2026. The article highlights that falling out-of-pocket expenditure shares mask unmet public spending targets, rural specialist shortages, and high outpatient healthcare costs. 
 For Prelims: NHA 2023-24 , Ayushman Arogya Mandirs , Antimicrobial Resistance , AB-PMJAY , Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission , eSanjeevani , Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana , Maternal Mortality Ratio , Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Vaccination , CAR-T Therapy , NexCAR19 , Diethylene Glycol . 
 For Mains: Key developments made in India's healthcare sector, Challenges associated and measures India can adopt to strengthen the healthcare sector. 
 National Health Accounts (NHA) 2023-24 show out-of-pocket expenditure (OOPE) falling from 64.2% to 42.7% , while government spending hit ₹4.14 trillion —though at 1.43% of GDP , it misses the National Health Policy 2017 2.5% target. Ayushman Arogya Mandirs , digital ecosystems, biomedical innovation, and maternal/TB gains drive transformation. Yet outpatient costs, rural specialist deficits, antimicrobial resistance , and climate risks persist. Achieving Universal Health Coverage (UHC) demands equity-weighted financing and integrated care.    
 What are the Key Developments Made in India's Healthcare Sector?   
 Stronger Financial Protection and Wider Health Assurance: India has expanded public health financing and risk pooling , advancing towards Universal Health Coverage (UHC).    
 The National Health Accounts 2023–24, released in November 2026, show that government health expenditure increased from ₹1.30 lakh crore in 2013–14 to ₹4.14 lakh crore in 2023–24, while households’ out-of-pocket expenditure (OOPE) declined from 64.2% in 2013-14 to 42.7% in 2023–24 of total health expenditure.    
 Meanwhile, AB-PMJAY had facilitated over 13 crore hospital admissions by September 2026, and its extension to everyone aged 70 years and above , irrespective of income, has strengthened geriatric financial protection . These admissions represent treatment episodes, rather than unique patients.     
 Expansion of Comprehensive Primary Healthcare and Last-Mile Access: Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (AAMs) have widened the scope of community healthcare to include non-communicable disease screening, mental healthcare, elderly care and palliative services .    
 India reported 1,87,250 AAMs as of October 2026 . Their expanded service framework includes essential drug and diagnostic lists covering 172 medicines and 63 diagnostics at PHC-level AAMs .    
 The equity dimension is significant. 30,817 AAMs in tribal districts were operational by December 2025. This creates a stronger foundation for early detection, longitudinal care and timely referral closer to underserved communities.     
 Digital Health Infrastructure and Remote Clinical Access: The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) is building an ecosystem for interoperable health records , while eSanjeevani expands access to remote consultations.    
 By September 2026, over 121 crore health records had been linked within ABDM. Separately, eSanjeevani crossed 50 crore cumulative teleconsultations in September 2026, supported by over 1.42 lakh AAM spokes and 19,473 medical hubs .    
 Its hub-and-spoke model connects frontline facilities with doctors remotely, helping address geographical barriers.     
 Larger Medical Training Capacity and Decentralised Specialist Infrastructure: India has substantially expanded its health workforce pipeline and teaching infrastructure.    
 A parliamentary reply in August 2026 reported 846 medical colleges , compared with 387 before 2014 , and 1,39,864 MBBS seats , compared with 51,348 .    
 Expansion also extends to specialist services. 71 of 75 approved super-speciality block projects under the Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana were complete.    
 Upgrading district and referral hospitals into teaching institutions can strengthen regional clinical capacity , medical training and access to advanced treatment.     
 Improved Maternal and Child Survival through a Continuum of Care: Progress is visible in measurable population health outcomes .    
 According to the SRS Special Bulletin on Maternal Mortality in India, 2022–24, India’s Maternal Mortality Ratio declined from 130 deaths per lakh live births in 2014–16 to 87 in 2022–24 , while the SRS Statistical Report, 2024 recorded a decline in under-five mortality from 43 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2015 to 28 in 2024 .    
 Programmes such as Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyaan (PMSMA) and extended PMSMA strengthen specialist antenatal examinations, high-risk pregnancy identification and referral preparedness.     
 Advanced TB Diagnostics and Shorter Drug-Resistant Treatment: India’s tuberculosis response increasingly combines active case finding, molecular diagnosis and shorter treatment regimens .    
 By October 2026, the country reported over 9,800 rapid molecular testing facilities and 107 culture and drug-susceptibility laboratories , supporting earlier diagnosis and identification of drug resistance.    
 The six-month, all-oral BPaLM regimen — bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid and moxifloxacin —has been introduced for eligible patients with drug-resistant TB, shortening treatment compared with older regimens lasting up to 18–20 months .   
 Extension of Immunisation into Adolescent Cancer Prevention: India has widened preventive healthcare through the nationwide Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Vaccination Campaign , launched in February 2026 for eligible 14-year-old girls .    
 By September 2026 , more than 80 lakh HPV vaccine doses had been administered free of cost.    
 This expands vaccination beyond its conventional maternal and early-childhood focus into adolescent health and cancer prevention .     
 Advances in Precision Medicine and Translation of Biomedical Research: India has progressed in cell and gene therapies , strengthening the connection between domestic research and clinical treatment.    
 A March 2026 parliamentary reply confirmed that the CAR-T therapies , NexCAR19 and Qartemi , were commercially available for specific blood cancers.    
 Their clinical reach is also widening. Homi Bhabha Cancer Hospital and Research Centre, New Chandigarh, reported three CAR-T infusions and 15 stem-cell transplants by September 2026.   
 What are the Key Challenges Associated with India’s Healthcare Sector?   
 High Treatment Costs and Incomplete Financial Protection: Healthcare expenditure continues to expose households to catastrophic spending, indebtedness and medical impoverishment .    
 The NSS 80 th Round Health Survey, 2025 , released in April 2026, estimated average out-of-pocket medical expenditure per hospitalisation, excluding childbirth, at ₹50,508 in private hospitals , compared with ₹6,631 in public facilities .    
 Repeated spending on medicines, diagnostics and outpatient consultations adds to this burden, particularly for patients with chronic diseases.     
 Rural Specialist Deficits and Unequal Workforce Distribution: India’s expanding medical education capacity has yet to resolve geographical maldistribution, specialist shortages and weak rural retention .    
 Parliamentary committee observations published in August 2026 highlighted a 70–80% shortfall of specialists at rural Community Health Centres , alongside the concentration of practitioners in urban centres.    
 Shortages of surgeons, physicians, obstetricians and paediatricians weaken referral services and emergency treatment. This creates a persistent gap between physical infrastructure and functional service availability .   
 Rising Chronic Disease Burden and Inadequate Continuity of Care: The epidemiological transition towards cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, cancer and chronic respiratory conditions demands sustained longitudinal care , regular medication and rehabilitation.    
 A 2026 OECD assessment estimated that these four disease groups account for 28% of premature deaths—deaths before age 75—in India .    
 Weak follow-up, fragmented referrals and interrupted medicine supplies can allow manageable conditions to progress into complications, increasing both specialist demand and household expenditure.     
 Large Mental Health Treatment Gaps and Weak Community Support: Stigma, delayed help-seeking, uneven specialist availability and inadequate rehabilitation leave substantial mental health needs unmet.    
 The National Mental Health Survey 2015–16 estimated treatment gaps ranging from 70% to 92% across different disorders . Their continuing policy relevance was reinforced by a March 2026 Health Ministry consultation , which highlighted inadequate advanced neuropsychiatric facilities in North India.     
 Antimicrobial Resistance and Shrinking Treatment Options: Antibiotic misuse, inappropriate prescribing and inadequate infection prevention make bacterial infections harder and more expensive to treat.    
 The NCDC’s January–June 2026 surveillance bulletin reported meropenem resistance in 62% of tested Klebsiella blood isolates and methicillin resistance in 60% of Staphylococcus aureus blood isolates .    
 Such resistance threatens the safety of intensive care, surgery, cancer chemotherapy and neonatal treatment , where effective antibiotics are essential.     
 Drug Quality Failures and Uneven Regulatory Enforcement: Ensuring Good Manufacturing Practices , batch traceability and rapid product recalls remains a major patient-safety challenge.    
 In October 2025, the Health Ministry confirmed that a tested sample of Coldrif cough syrup contained diethylene glycol beyond permissible limits, prompting regulatory action.    
 A March 2026 parliamentary reply reported over 860 regulatory actions following risk-based inspections of more than 960 manufacturing premises since December 2022.    
 Divided responsibilities across central and state regulators make timely interstate alerts and coordinated action particularly important.   
 Climate-Related Health Risks and Inadequate Facility Preparedness: Extreme heat places additional demands on emergency services, reliable electricity, water supplies and cooling infrastructure , while threatening vulnerable patients and outdoor workers.    
 The NCDC’s review of 2024 heat-health activities recorded 48,156 suspected heatstroke cases . Among facilities assessed during April–July 2024, only 32% reported emergency cooling preparedness .     
 Digital Exclusion and Unequal Access to Technology-Enabled Care: Digital health expansion faces persistent gender gaps, uneven digital literacy and dependence on shared devices .    
 The Comprehensive Modular Survey: Telecom, January–March 2025, found that only 57.6% of rural women aged 15 and above had used the internet during the preceding three months, compared with 72.1% of rural men .    
 These disparities can hinder access to online appointments, electronic records and remote consultations , particularly for older people and women without personal devices.    
 What Measures can India Adopt to Strengthen the Healthcare Sector?   
 Make Public Financing Predictable and Equity-Weighted: The Centre and states should adopt rolling three-year health financing agreements , with district allocations reflecting poverty, disease burden, tribal populations and travel time to facilities .    
 Essential staffing, medicines and maintenance should receive protected funding, while a smaller improvement grant rewards independently verified gains in service quality. Districts starting with weaker infrastructure should receive additional support.    
 Direct facility financing , accompanied by public expenditure dashboards and community audits, would give managers greater flexibility to resolve local shortages.     
 Purchase Complete Care Pathways and Extend Outpatient Protection: States should pilot cashless outpatient benefit packages covering consultations, essential diagnostics, medicines and follow-up, beginning with vulnerable households and conditions requiring repeated treatment.    
 Each participating household should have a designated primary care team responsible for coordinating referrals and post-discharge care. Providers could receive risk-adjusted capitation—a fixed payment per enrolled person—combined with quality incentives for treatment continuity and appropriate referrals.     
 Build Rural Clinical Teams through Career-Linked Service Packages: States should offer voluntary rural service contracts combining predictable tenure, hardship allowances, safe accommodation, continuing education and transparent career progression.    
 Recruitment should ensure that facilities receive functioning teams comprising doctors, nurses, laboratory personnel and other essential professionals. Regional specialist pools could provide scheduled rotations and emergency backup, supported by reliable referral transport.    
 Competency-based task sharing , within legally authorised scopes of practice, would help qualified nurses and allied professionals undertake defined responsibilities.     
 Integrate Chronic Disease and Mental Healthcare into Routine Services: Primary care networks should introduce shared care plans for patients with overlapping conditions such as diabetes, hypertension and depression.    
 Trained counsellors should deliver structured psychological interventions under supervision, with stepped-care referral for severe illness or inadequate improvement.    
 Follow-up should assess disease control, functioning and treatment adherence , alongside detection.     
 Make Patient Safety a Condition of Healthcare Purchasing: Government purchasers should include measurable infection prevention, antimicrobial stewardship and medication-safety obligations in hospital contracts, backed by funding for compliance.    
 Hospitals should review selected antibiotic prescriptions after 48–72 hours , use local resistance data and report serious preventable incidents through protected reporting systems.    
 Drug procurement contracts should require batch-level traceability and enable rapid quarantine and recall after validated contamination alerts. Independent audits should examine corrective action and patient outcomes.    
 Guarantee Assisted Digital Access and Independently Validate Clinical AI: Every public facility should provide assisted registration, local-language interfaces and accessible alternatives for patients without smartphones or digital skills.    
 Essential treatment should remain accessible when identity authentication or connectivity fails. Digital systems should support interoperability, purpose-limited data access and auditable consent .    
 Before purchasing clinical AI, states should require multicentre external validation across relevant populations and facility types, followed by monitored deployment with clinician oversight.     
 Link Indigenous Innovation and Procurement to Demonstrated Health Value: India should establish problem-led innovation challenges for underserved needs, followed by independent clinical evaluation and competitive procurement of successful solutions.    
 Health Technology Assessment (HTA) should guide major coverage and purchasing decisions by assessing safety, clinical benefit, affordability and equity.    
 Device contracts should include maintenance, consumables, staff training and uptime guarantees . HTA India already evaluates medicines, devices and digital interventions , providing an institutional foundation for this proposed expansion.   
 Conclusion    
 India’s healthcare trajectory demonstrates commendable strides in financial protection, primary care expansion, digital health infrastructure, and indigenous precision medicine. However, realizing genuine Universal Health Coverage demands shifting from episodic hospitalisation coverage to comprehensive, continuous care . Addressing rural specialist deficits, outpatient medicine costs, antimicrobial resistance, and climate-induced facility vulnerabilities through equity-weighted public financing and strict regulatory accountability will build a resilient, patient-centred health system.    
 Drishti Mains Question 
 Despite improvements in health financing and service delivery, India continues to face significant healthcare inequalities. Analyse the major challenges and suggest suitable reforms.  
 Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)   
 1. What does the NHA 2023–24 reveal about OOPE?   
 OOPE declined from 64.2% to 42.7% of total health expenditure, while government health expenditure rose to ₹4.14 lakh crore.   
 2. What is the significance of Ayushman Arogya Mandirs?    
 They expand primary healthcare to include NCD screening, mental health, elderly care, and palliative services, with 1,87,250 AAMs operational.   
 3. What are India's key maternal and child health achievements?    
 MMR declined from 130 (2014–16) to 87 (2022–24) per lakh live births; under-five mortality fell from 43 to 28 per 1,000.   
 4. What are NexCAR19 and Qartemi?  
 NexCAR19 and Qartemi are commercially available CAR-T cell therapies in India for specified blood cancers.   
 5. What is the eSanjeevani teleconsultation milestone?   
 It crossed 50 crore cumulative teleconsultations in September 2026 through a hub-and-spoke model with 19,473 medical hubs.   
 UPSC Civil Services Examination, Previous Year Questions (PYQs)   
 Prelims   
 Q. Which of the following are the objectives of ‘National Nutrition Mission’? (2017) 
 To create awareness relating to malnutrition among pregnant women and lactating mothers.     
 To reduce the incidence of anaemia among young children, adolescent girls and women.     
 To promote the consumption of millets, coarse cereals and unpolished rice.     
 To promote the consumption of poultry eggs.     
 Select the correct answer using the code given below:     
 (a) 1 and 2 only      
 (b) 1, 2 and 3 only      
 (c) 1, 2 and 4 only       
 (d) 3 and 4 only      
 Ans: (a) 
 Mains     
 Q. How do you account for the growing fast food industries given that there are increased health concerns in modern society? Illustrate your answer with the Indian experience. (2025)

 Q. “Besides being a moral imperative of a Welfare State, primary health structure is a necessary precondition for sustainable development.” Analyse. (2021) 
 Q. In order to enhance the prospects of social development, sound and adequate healthcare policies are needed particularly in the fields of geriatric and maternal healthcare. Discuss (2020) 
 Q. Despite Consistent experience of high growth, India still goes with the lowest indicators of human development. Examine the issues that make balanced and inclusive development elusive. (2019)  
 Q. Appropriate local community-level healthcare intervention is a prerequisite to achieve 'Health for All' in India. Explain. (2018)
